title: Remote entanglement of massive oscillators via wire-mediated Coulomb interaction
authors: Lorenzo Papa, Onur Hosten, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero
abstract: We propose a method to enhance Coulomb interaction between charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators by placing a conducting structure in their vicinity. We derive the effective motional dynamics of the two oscillators using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and show that image charges induced in the conductor fundamentally modify the range of the electrostatic interaction. For the specific case of a cylindrical wire, we predict that the coherent motional coupling changes from the free-space scaling $1/D^3$ to an asymptotic $1/(D\ln^2 D)$ dependence on the separation $D$ between the oscillators, at the cost of only negligible additional decoherence for low-frequency oscillators. We further show that, when combined with continuous position measurements, the enhanced interaction enables the generation of steady-state motional entanglement between the oscillators over significantly larger distances than achievable in free space. For experimentally realistic milligram-scale oscillators, we predict observable entanglement at separations of several hundred microns -- more than an order of magnitude beyond free-space capabilities -- with improvements approaching two orders of magnitude in future systems. These results identify conductor-assisted Coulomb interactions as a resource for quantum control of massive objects and for the exploration of entanglement generated by fundamental central forces.
summary: The paper demonstrates how placing charged macroscopic oscillators near a conducting wire fundamentally alters their Coulomb interaction, enhancing the coupling strength at large separations. By combining this enhanced interaction with continuous position measurements, the authors show that steady-state motional entanglement can be generated over distances far exceeding free-space limits. This establishes conductor-assisted interactions as a novel resource for quantum control.
main_problem: The authors propose a method to enhance the Coulomb interaction between massive mechanical oscillators by placing them near a conducting structure, aiming to generate steady-state motional entanglement over long distances.
main_result: They predict that the wire modifies the coupling scaling from $1/D^3$ to $1/(D\ln^2 D)$, enabling observable entanglement at separations much larger than achievable in free space.
method: The analysis uses macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, deriving effective dynamics via a master equation approach and employing continuous measurement theory (Kalman filtering analogy).
model_or_system: The system consists of two charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators coupled by both free-space Coulomb interaction and an image charge interaction mediated by a nearby conducting wire. The dynamics are described by a Hamiltonian and subsequently analyzed using a master equation.
key_observables: Steady-state motional entanglement, renormalized mechanical frequency ($\Omega'_f$), and the modified coupling rate ($G_{	ext{tot}}$).
important_parameters: Separation $D$, oscillator mass $m$, wire geometry (cylindrical), and operating regime (low-frequency limit $\hbar\Omega \ll k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the electroquasistatic limit, linearizes position dependence around equilibrium points, and utilizes approximations like Born-Markov for bath tracing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup showing image charge generation; one figure compares coupling rates vs. distance $D$ (free space vs. wire); another shows rate dependencies on separation and proximity to instability.
paper_structure: The paper develops from deriving the effective Hamiltonian incorporating medium effects, leading to a master equation description of dynamics, simplifying this master equation using approximations like RWA, and finally analyzing state evolution under continuous measurement via Kalman filtering analogies.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum control of massive objects by engineering long-range interactions, which is highly relevant for cavity QED and open quantum systems research involving mechanical resonators.
